chapter_theme: Songs at Thiruthuraiyur (திருத்துறையூர்): the poet asks whether company with ornamented singing women befits him, and fears fate, Death's rope, the pyre and hell; he asks for the flower feet, and praises Murugan as the guru who taught and as lord of the shrine where gods and sages receive grace.
structure_note: Two songs: 741 on women and Murugan as guru, 742 a long confession of fate, death and the pyre.

741.reading: The poet describes women who hold a yaazh and sing while their cloth and hair slip, scented with rosewater and civet, with earrings swaying, eyes like spears and carp, lips like sugar and kovai fruit, voices like cuckoos and waists like thread, and asks whether he should keep company with these maddening women of fickle anger. The praise names Sivakami, the goddess the devotees worship, and Murugan as the guru who taught one joined to Bhadrakali, as the hero whose vel struck Sura's mountain and sea, and as the lord of the shining hunter girl at Thuraiyur.
741.nuance: பித்தர்கள் உறவாமோ closes the description with a question rather than a plea. The line பூமிக்கடல் மூவர்க்கு முன்னாள் பத்திரகாளிப் புணர் போகர்க்கு உபதேசித்தருள் குருநாதா makes Murugan a teacher, but whom he taught is unclear: போகர் may be Siva as Bhadrakali's consort or the siddha Bhogar, and the first words do not split with certainty.

742.reading: The poet says that through many forms and births, in a womb-pit made of deeds, he has learned the elders' word that fate cannot be turned aside; he fears the hour when he is seized and bound with rope, the body becomes a heap of worms, is melted like wax and burned with rising smoke, becomes food for hell, while his kin stand at the door weeping, and asks to be freed from these and given the flower feet of grace to bow to. The praise names Murugan of the vel on the galloping peacock, who gives grace at Thuraiyur to sages, siddhas, Maheswaras, Hari and Brahma.
742.nuance: விதியாரும் விலக்கவொணாது எனும் முதியோர் சொல்: the poet cites, and accepts, the proverb that no one can avert fate, and the plea is to escape it by grace. உபாதிகள், afflictions, is the word for the whole chain from rope to pyre. Several lines (சாதக விதம், மகாகட சலதாரை, சதிகாரர் விடக்கு) are hard to split, so the order of events is a reading.

links.note: The Kural says nothing is stronger than fate, which arrives before any scheme to avert it; 742 cites the same elders' word and grants it (தகவாம் அது), yet asks for the Lord's grace to free him from what fate brings. Not a tension, since the poet does not deny the saying: grace is set beside fate as the one thing no human scheme is.

742 fears the hour when the body is burned with rising smoke, becomes food for hell, and kin stand at the door with sinking hearts (தலைக்கடை போய் எதிர் உளமாழ்கி). Tirumanthiram 145 has the town wail, call the man a corpse, burn him and bathe and forget him (நினைப்பொழிந்தார்களே). Both stage the death scene with the mourners; the Tirumanthiram ends on their forgetting, the song on the poet's plea to escape by grace.
